title: Reuters/Ipsos Poll: 63% Say Trump Family’s Crypto Profits Were Inappropriate
description_medium: A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted August 14–17, 2026 found that 63% of U.S. adults considered it inappropriate for President Donald Trump and his family to profit from cryptocurrency ventures; 32% said it was appropriate. Separately, 69% said Trump’s private business interests influenced his presidential decisions. The survey measured respondents’ views, not proof of a particular decision being made for personal gain.
description_long:
A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted online from August 14 to 17, 2026 asked 1,166 U.S. adults about President Donald Trump’s private business interests and cryptocurrency ventures. Sixty-three percent said it was inappropriate for Trump and his family to have profited from cryptocurrency since his return to office, while 32% considered the profits appropriate. The poll also asked a separate question about influence: 69% said Trump’s private business interests were influencing his presidential decisions. These are distinct findings; the 69% figure does not measure whether crypto profits were appropriate.

The poll appeared amid Trump family activity in digital assets, including the president’s promotion of his self-branded crypto coin in March 2025. The survey records public perceptions of ethical boundaries and potential conflicts between personal business and public office. It does not establish that any specific presidential action was affected by those interests, determine the amount of family profit, or make a legal finding of wrongdoing. The results also varied by party: Reuters reported that about three in ten Republican respondents viewed the crypto profits as inappropriate, while seven in ten said they were appropriate. The findings therefore show both broad public concern and substantial partisan division.

corrected_wording.corrected: 63% said the Trump family’s cryptocurrency profits were inappropriate; separately, 69% said his private business interests influenced his presidential decisions.

source_access_notes: Reuters article opened and used as the poll source; USA Today and Rappler links were attached references. Wording distinguishes the two reported questions.
rationale: Replaced repeated and conflated poll wording with the separate 63% crypto appropriateness and 69% business-influence results; clarified that a poll is not evidence of an actual decision or legal violation.

title: IBTimes Reports Disputed Epstein-Related Tape Claim About Trump
description_medium: An August 2026 IBTimes UK article revisited Sarah Ransome’s older claim that Jeffrey Epstein had recordings involving Donald Trump and other prominent people. The article says no tapes have been produced or independently verified, and that Ransome’s account has previously been challenged. It distinguishes that claim from separate FBI interview notes and court records discussed in the same report.
description_long:
An August 19, 2026 IBTimes UK article revisited a claim by Sarah Ransome, an associate of Epstein victim Virginia Giuffre, that Jeffrey Epstein recorded sexual encounters involving prominent people, including Donald Trump. Ransome has said recordings existed and were used as leverage, but the article reports that no tapes have been publicly produced or independently verified and that her account has previously been challenged. The story circulated again on social media, where it was presented as newly surfaced evidence.

The article also discusses separate materials: FBI interview notes in which a woman alleged that Trump assaulted her when she was a minor, and a lawsuit concerning another plaintiff’s alleged abuse by Epstein. Those records and allegations are distinct from Ransome’s tape claim. The article says the lawsuit did not name the prominent man accused in the alleged assault, and it does not establish that the tape claim is corroborated by the FBI notes or court filings. Trump has denied the broader controversy, calling it a hoax, according to the article. The available reporting therefore documents that the allegation resurfaced, while leaving the claimed recordings unverified; it does not establish that they exist or that the alleged encounters occurred.

corrected_wording.claim: “Secret tapes show Trump in alleged sexual encounters”
corrected_wording.corrected: Sarah Ransome has claimed recordings existed, but no tapes have been produced or independently verified; the IBTimes article distinguishes this from separate FBI and court records.

source_access_notes: Opened attached IBTimes UK article. It explicitly states the purported recordings have not been produced or verified and distinguishes them from separate documentary allegations.
rationale: Corrected the entry’s false implication that the tapes are in court files or constitute verified evidence, while preserving the article’s actual news angle: an old disputed claim resurfaced.

title: Sessions Directs Border Prosecutors to Pursue Nearly All Illegal-Entry Referrals
description_medium: On April 6, 2018, Attorney General Jeff Sessions directed five U.S. Attorney’s Offices along the Southwest border to prosecute all Department of Homeland Security referrals for unlawful entry under 8 U.S.C. § 1325(a), to the extent practicable. Criminal prosecution of parents contributed to family separations because children could not accompany adults into federal criminal detention. The policy increased separations, according to the Government Accountability Office.
description_long:
Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced the “zero tolerance” policy on April 6, 2018. His directive told U.S. Attorney’s Offices in California, Arizona, New Mexico and the two federal districts in Texas along the Southwest border to prosecute all Department of Homeland Security referrals for violations of 8 U.S.C. § 1325(a), covering attempted or completed unlawful entry, “to the extent practicable.” That changed the enforcement approach by calling for criminal prosecution of nearly every referred adult rather than prioritizing only selected cases.

Because children could not be held with parents in federal criminal custody, the increased prosecutions separated many families. The Government Accountability Office later reported that the memo increased the rate of separations and placed more children in the custody of the Office of Refugee Resettlement. It also found that DHS and Health and Human Services officials had not planned for the resulting increase and said they did not know about the memo before its public release. In June 2018, a federal judge ordered reunifications; the government identified 2,654 children for potential reunification, and 437 remained in custody as of September 10, according to GAO. These figures describe that court-ordered reunification effort, not necessarily every separation under the policy. The administration halted referrals of parents under the policy later that June.
source_access_notes: Opened the Justice Department release and used GAO-19-163 for separation and reunification context.
rationale: Adds what the directive required and explains the causal link to family separation with GAO findings, without implying the DOJ release itself documented downstream effects.

title: Trump Sets Safeguard Tariffs on Solar Imports and Residential Washers
description_medium: On January 23, 2018, President Donald Trump approved Section 201 safeguard tariffs on imported solar cells and modules and large residential washing machines after the International Trade Commission found that increased imports were causing serious injury to U.S. manufacturers. Solar tariffs began at 30% and declined to 15% over four years, with the first 2.5 gigawatts of imported cells exempt each year. Washer duties varied by quota and fell over three years.
description_long:
President Donald Trump approved safeguard tariffs on imported solar cells and modules and large residential washers on January 23, 2018, after the U.S. International Trade Commission found that increased imports were a substantial cause of serious injury to domestic manufacturers. The measures used different tariff schedules for the two industries. Solar cells and modules faced a 30% tariff in the first year, declining to 25%, 20% and 15% in the following years; the first 2.5 gigawatts of imported solar cells were exempt annually.

For finished washers, the tariff-rate quota set a 20% duty on the first 1.2 million imported units in year one and 50% on units above that threshold. Those rates declined to 18% and 45% in year two, then 16% and 40% in year three. Covered washer parts also faced duties, with specified quantities exempt. U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer said the ITC found that washer imports had risen steadily from 2012 to 2016 while domestic producers’ financial performance declined sharply. The administration framed the safeguard actions as temporary relief for U.S. manufacturers. These were import tariffs, not a general ban; the schedules applied to covered products and included defined thresholds and exceptions. The decision followed a trade-remedy investigation and recommendations to the president, rather than a blanket tariff on all trade with the countries supplying those goods.
source_access_notes: The attached White House archive URL returned 404; used the USTR press release reproducing the official approved schedules and ITC findings.
rationale: Provides source-backed tariff rates, quotas, duration and the ITC rationale after the attached event URL was unavailable.

title: MS NOW Reports GOP Investigators Deflect Questions on Trump Family Finances
description_medium: An MS NOW report published August 20, 2026, contrasted Republican investigations of former President Joe Biden and his family with lawmakers’ responses to possible self-dealing by the Trump family. The available summary says some former Biden investigators described such scrutiny as someone else’s responsibility. This is a report about political oversight and lawmakers’ stated roles, not a finding of criminal conduct.
description_long:
MS NOW’s report compared Republican lawmakers’ intense scrutiny of former President Joe Biden and his family with their responses to questions about potential self-dealing by the Trump family. The available summary says lawmakers who led Biden investigations were now saying it was someone else’s job to investigate the Trump family. This juxtaposition is the article’s central political criticism: lawmakers who once pursued oversight energetically appeared to disclaim responsibility when scrutiny turned toward the current president’s family.

The report’s headline calls these Republicans “silent,” while its synopsis describes a more specific response: deflecting responsibility for an investigation. That distinction matters because a claim about lawmakers’ statements and committee roles is narrower than a claim that they made no public comment at all. The story concerns the consistency of congressional oversight and the contrast in how members of the same party approached allegations involving two presidential families. It does not establish that the Trump family engaged in illegal conduct or that the Biden investigations proved wrongdoing by Joe Biden. The report’s comparison is political analysis of lawmakers’ conduct, rather than a judicial or investigative finding about either family.

corrected_wording.claim: “The same Republicans are silent on Trump self-dealing”
corrected_wording.corrected: MS NOW reported that some Republicans who led Biden-family investigations said scrutiny of possible Trump-family self-dealing was someone else’s responsibility; the broad “silent” wording is the outlet’s characterization.

source_access_notes: MS NOW URL was blocked by robots.txt. Search results and an accessible syndication listing supplied only the article summary and publication date; no additional named examples are stated.
blockers: The linked MS NOW article body was inaccessible. Full text is needed to verify named lawmakers, business examples, quotes and responses.
rationale: Provides the narrow point supported by the indexed synopsis and labels the article’s headline as framing; the incomplete source prevents a fuller event description.
